summary:
Central Java is a province of Indonesia, and a visitor there stands under Indonesia's national legal framework. The sources record no provision specific to Central Java that would alter that position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X marker on identity documents, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

The national penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls within the outside-marital-sex restriction. Reporting indicates prosecutions under the provision are selective rather than systematic.

Physical risk to transgender visitors is rising. Reporting in August 2026 documents growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community, and other reporting ties a surge in vigilante mob attacks on transgender people to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, go further than the national framework and criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025, and two men were flogged in Aceh in January 2021. Central Java has no equivalent provincial provision in the sources, but a visitor travelling onward to those provinces carries the exposure with them.

Raids on transgender people have been carried out by administrative bodies rather than police alone: the Jakarta Social Agency has conducted raids on transgender women in the capital district. The pattern of official action against LGBT people is national in scope, not confined to the provinces known for religious bylaws.

Indonesia's international standing on the issue is contested. The 2022 penal code drew international criticism, including from the United Nations, for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and for domestic partnerships.
localsOnly:
Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP). Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth-gender descriptor is printed unless a court order was already obtained; electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces.

Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, which shapes local expectations in Central Java even as national policy hardens.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Central Java provincial regulation, local bylaws, or police practice within Central Java itself; the province's position is derived entirely from the national framework, and any local provision would be unresolved here.

The penalty for sex outside marriage is reported inconsistently across sources, at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year on complaint by an immediate family member. Which figure applies in which procedural circumstance is not resolved by the inventory.

Enforcement of the outside-marital-sex provision is described as selective rather than systematic, but no prosecution data for Central Java is sourced. The status and final text of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour is also unresolved.

Whether national police have conducted raids on LGBT gatherings within Central Java is not sourced; the documented raids are from other provinces.
